newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Bleak year for race relations in U.S..
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Bleak year for race relations in U.S..

text.p: It was a year when polls said white Americans might elect a black man president if given the chance and a year when two books came out with the same dire warning in their titles -- "The Coming Race War".

It was also a year when Californians voted to end affirmative action, or positive discrimination, programmes to aid minorities and a year when a shamed Texaco oil company admitted it discriminated against black employees -- "black jellybeans" as one executive called them -- and agreed to pay $140 million in damages.

And it was a year when a Republican Congress and a Democratic president declared war on welfare, throwing those programmes back to the states to administer and putting a time limit on help. It was a measure many critics saw as aimed chiefly at the national symbol of those on welfare -- young, unmarried, black mothers.
SPECTRE OF SIMPSON TRIAL
Hovering over a sour year for U.S. race relations, never out of sight, was the lingering racial bitterness of the O.J. Simpson murder trial.

White and black Americans began 1996 starkly divided with whites convinced that a mostly black jury had allowed the famed black athlete to get away with murder at his 1995 criminal trial, while most blacks were convinced he had been framed by a racist police force.

Now Simpson is being tried before a predominantly white jury in a civil damages suit brought by relatives of his murdered ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman. The case continues to divide Americans along racial lines. Many blacks wonder why he is being tried twice, while many whites root for him to be found guilty this time.

Ted Shaw of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People's (NAACP) Legal Defence Fund said a white blacklash against the verdict in the Simpson case may have been a factor in California voters' approval of Proposition 209, a measure designed to end affirmative action programmes in that state, which passed by a vote of 54 to 46 percent.
"Obviously the Simpson trial and verdict revealed deep fault lines on racial grounds in California and elsewhere and we continue to see those fault lines exhibited," he said.

Shaw called 1996 "not a good year for civil rights". Political scientist Andrew Hacker, an expert on America's racial divide, used sharper language, calling 1996 a continuation of "the crackdown on African Americans."

"White Americans have decided that enough is enough. They want longer prison sentences, want welfare mothers to go out and work. White America is tired of hearing about racism and say: "We have done enough,'" Hacker said, summing up the mood of 1996, a year that marked the 100th anniversary of Plessy versus Ferguson, the Supreme Court decision that ushered in an era of American apartheid -- legalised segregation.
COLIN POWELL FACTOR

One bright note in a bleak picture was the enthusiasm shown by white America at the possibility that retired General Colin Powell might run for president. Powell, the first black chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, declared himself a Republican and teased the party with the prospect of running.

Polls, even one taken the day President Bill Clinton was re-elected, showed Powell had enough support to win the presidency. But he did not run and his wife said she feared someone would try to assassinate him if he did.

In another political note, several black members of Congress won re-election even after their mainly black districts were ruled unconstitutional and redrawn with more white voters. In winning in white majority districts, many claimed that was proof racism was dead in America, but others maintained they won because of the power of incumbency.

Hacker called Powell "a white creation" and maintained that white people found him attractive because he was the kind of black who didn't get angry, didn't threaten them and, in the end, a man they didn't have to vote for.

But whatever Powell's merits, he was a product of a system many white Americans want to see disappear -- affirmative action. He was named a general by a secretary of the army who rejected the first promotion lists given him because they did not contain a single black name.
RACIAL TENSION

Columnist Carl Rowan, a noted black journalist and author of the "The Coming Race War in America," says racial hostility lies just beneath the surface and can erupt at any time. "All you need is a few nuts and the problem can burst out. Some of these militia nuts say they can get a race war going by assassinating 10 or 12 black leaders," Rowan said.

Indeed, 1996 saw incidents of racial violence from arson fires that destroyed more than three dozen black churches to riots in St Petersburg, Florida, over the death of a black motorist shot by a white policeman after a traffic stop.
University of Colorado law professor Richard Degado, author of "The Coming Race War?", says he sees more violence and more polarisation in the years ahead.

Echoing Hacker's thesis of a crackdown on African Americans, he said: "I think that white folks in high places have decided across the country to take a stand because they believe that blacks and Latinos are getting too big for their britches.

"Behind all this is the fear that by the year 2020, whites will be a minority in this country. So there has been a stiffening of the spine, a feeling that it is time to seize control before things get out of hand."
